label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
**4 stars. Good camera, honest limits — just know what problem you're solving.**

We streamed worship on a $70 webcam from 2020 until this past winter. It worked the way most of us expect things to work, which is to say it mostly didn't. So when the board approved money for a real camera, we paid $2,140 to Chancel AV for a Lindqvist Optics PT-20 in February, and $95 more for a wall mount.

The installation is where the money was well spent. One PoE cable up to the balcony — that's the only cable, which matters in a building our 1920s electrical plan treats as a suggestion. The PT-20 gives us 20x optical zoom and 1080p60, and it feeds both HDMI and NDI HX, so it runs into OBS on the old office PC and out to our YouTube channel. We get 30 to 60 viewers most Sundays, which for us is the whole sanctuary on a good week and about half the county on holidays.

The thing I did not expect to care about as much as I do: presets. We have nine stored — altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide shot, and two on the chancel steps. Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, runs the thing off the free web app on a tablet and learned it in one afternoon. Somebody with no tech background can do this. That is not a small thing for a church with a volunteer staff of two.

Picture quality is genuinely good in normal light. The zoom holds up across our 92-foot nave in a way the webcam could never have approached — you can frame the font and still see the chancel. Two honest complaints. First, on the first Sunday the presets drifted a few degrees by the time we got to the sermon, so the pulpit shot was aimed a little into the wall. A firmware update (2.4, in March) fixed it and it has not happened since. Second, autofocus hunts when someone walks between the camera and the pulpit, so we lock focus on each preset and live with that. If your people move around during the service, know that.

Where it surprised us was Easter Vigil. The candlelit service, the first *Christ the Lord Is Risen Today* with only candles. The picture got grainy — noticeably grainy — but it stayed usable. The webcam that morning showed nothing but dots. The vigil was broadcast, people watched it, and afterward Delores, who is 82 and no longer comes to church, called to say she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That is the whole review, really, but it isn't the whole picture.

Two things people should know before they spend the money. The manual is thin and badly translated — the preset workflow in particular took some poking around to figure out. Chancel AV's tech support was excellent; Marcy walked me through it on the phone, twice, without making me feel like a nuisance. Call them. Second, and I want to be plain about this: audio is not the camera's job, and this camera did nothing for our sound problem. If your streaming setup sounds bad, a better camera will not fix it. We still have a sound system that hums when the HVAC kicks on, and no camera in the world will solve that.

Would I buy it again? Yes. But a congregation under 100 people, in a smaller room, streaming mostly to people who don't need to see the font — you could do fine with something cheaper, and I'd rather say so than have you spend $2,000 and feel foolish. We have a 92-foot nave and needed to see the altar. That need is what this price is for.

It is a good camera. It did what we needed and some of what we didn't know we needed. Four stars.
